title: AI-Fuzzy Markup Language with Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning
venue: 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on CI for High-School Student Learning
extended_summary:
This paper reports on the 2021 IEEE CIS Summer School on Computational Intelligence for High-School Student Learning and addresses how to introduce computational intelligence concepts to younger learners, especially high-school students, through a co-learning framework that combines human learning with AI and robotics. The authors position the work as part of outreach and education in computational intelligence, with a focus on helping pre-university students understand foundational concepts such as fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation.

The intervention combined lectures and hands-on AIoT workshops built around AI-Fuzzy Markup Language (AI-FML), the IEEE 1855 standard, and co-learning with devices such as the Kebbi Air robot, AIoT-FML-LT, and MoonCar. The paper also presents a machine-human co-learning model and a learning framework for workshops in which students used AI-FML learning tools, built or trained fuzzy-system knowledge and rule bases, interacted with robots, and explored real-world applications such as intelligent air conditioning, speaking English, and brain-computer interface applications.

The participant pool was broad rather than limited strictly to high-school students. Of 214 registrants, the sample included elementary, junior high, senior high, university, and graduate students, as well as teachers, parents, and other attendees from Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, and a small number from other countries. The event was conducted physically in Taiwan and virtually through Zoom, making the setting blended. Outcomes reported included attendance, certificate completion, submitted reports, and participant feedback.

The main conclusion is that the summer school and AIoT workshops were successful in engaging participants and helping them understand core computational intelligence concepts. Based on short reports and feedback surveys, the authors conclude that participants gained understanding of computational intelligence, fuzzy logic, neural networks, and evolutionary computation, and that the workshop provided useful experience applying AI-FML tools to real-world problems. However, the evidence is primarily descriptive and based on reports and feedback rather than rigorous learning assessments or controlled comparisons.
quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a descriptive report of a summer school and workshop with informal feedback, attendance counts, and anecdotal comments. It lacks a clear empirical study design, validated outcome measures, comparison group, or statistical analysis, so it does not meet credibility criteria for stronger evidence tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests positive but unclear impact on participants' understanding and motivation, with no reported effect sizes or rigorous causal evidence. Reported benefits are promising but too weakly measured to justify green or blue impact tiers.

interventions.use_case: High-school and younger students interacted with the AI-FML robot Kebbi Air during an AIoT workshop to explore fuzzy-system outputs, robot expressions, and human-robot co-learning activities.

Students used the AI-FML learning platform, AI-FML Lab, and Blockly-based tools to learn computational intelligence concepts and experiment with AIoT applications such as intelligent air conditioning, speaking English, and BCI demonstrations.
The workshop asked students to simulate robot perception/cognition and vary fuzzy-system and PSO parameters to observe effects on learning performance and system behavior in applied AIoT scenarios.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants' short reports and feedback surveys indicated they understood principles of computational intelligence, neural networks, fuzzy logic, and evolutionary computation to a higher degree than in previous summer schools. However, no validated pre/post assessment, statistical test, or effect size is reported, so the evidence is descriptive rather than causal. The total number attending at least two-thirds of lectures/workshops was 78, with 80 short reports and 77 feedback surveys submitted.
finding.measure: Participant short reports, feedback surveys, attendance/certificate completion, and informal judgments of understanding of computational intelligence concepts
finding.study_size: n=78 attendees completing at least two-thirds; n=80 reports; n=77 surveys

finding.finding_summary: Teacher and organizer feedback suggests the summer school and AIoT workshop increased student motivation and interest in computational intelligence, with comments describing the event as stimulating involvement in rapidly evolving fields and fostering future research interest. These findings are based on anecdotal feedback rather than standardized motivation measures, and no comparative statistics are provided.
finding.measure: Anecdotal teacher comments and participant feedback about motivation, engagement, and interest
finding.study_size: n=77 feedback surveys; qualitative remarks from teachers/participants

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents the summer school as a successful outreach model that expanded computational intelligence exposure to high-school and even elementary students across Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, and other countries. Institutional reach is evidenced by 214 registrants and international participation, but the paper does not provide formal evaluation of policy change, sustained adoption, or downstream institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Registration counts, cross-country participation, certificate completion, and narrative claims about outreach and alignment with STEM/education policy goals
